title: Breaking News! Nampa, Caldwell, and Canyon County Seek Alternativ - NewsBreak
text:
By Kevin Miller ,
2 hours ago
Despite the complete transparency of the West Valley Humane Society, the cities of Nampa, Caldwell, and Canyon County have decided to look at other alternatives to the shelter that has been underfunded by Nampa, Caldwell, and Canyon County for years.
The shelter would’ve closed if not for the work of the dedicated staff, volunteers, donors, and the massive monetary and staff donations from the Best Friends Animal Society, over $400,000, and the Idaho Humane Society, over $100,000.
(Editor’s note, author is a member of the West Valley Humane Society Board)
Without notice, the two cities and the county issued a press release asking for a Request for Proposals from West Valley and other shelters. In a recent meeting, the CEO of the Idaho Humane Society spoke before the Caldwell City Council, stating how great a deal the city was getting.
The county’s press release stated, “West Valley Humane Society (WVHS) requested a substantial increase in funding of $1.5 million total, with no room for negotiation.” One has to ask, what essential services are the cities and the county willing to cut to make their budgets?
The release reported how all entities have been worried about the care of animals at the shelter. ‘ Over the past two years, community members have raised concerns about animal health and wellness, veterinary care, adoption opportunities, and overall shelter operations.’
Although the shelter has needed help for years, there was never a question from Nampa or Caldwell about the amount spent on essential animal health and welfare.
The three entities will now review the applications from whoever submits the request for proposals. Regardless of who takes over the care of animals in Canyon County, let’s hope those responsible do the right thing by adequately funding the shelter.
Items Dangerous to Animals That You Have in Your Yard We spoke with Wild Care Cape Cod Executive Director Stephanie Ellis about the dangers of many everyday yard items and how they can affect the wildlife we know and love. Here are some of the dangers your yard may present to animals and how you can reduce their risk. Gallery Credit: Nancy Hall Ron Chapple studios Carved Pumpkins Yes, carving up a jack-o'-lantern is family fun every fall, but it can also lead to some serious sickness in pets and wildlife. As Stephanie Ellis of Wild Care Cape Cod informed us, "Don't leave moldy pumpkins out for decoration."
The carved pumpkins tend to rot faster than un-carved pumpkins and that can mean growing toxic fungi. If you notice your jack-o'-lanterns are getting moldy, it is time to get them off your porch. Both pets and wildlife have been known to take bites of moldy pumpkins and make themselves extremely sick. For animals both free and tamed, get the moldy pumpkins disposed of ASAP. Maria Symchych-Navrotska Halloween Decorations Halloween is a great time to deck out the yard for trick-or-treaters, but be careful what you decorate with. Though Ellis tells us they have yet to experience any Halloween decoration incidents with animals at Wild Care Cape Cod, she did say fake spider webs on bushes have been known to entangle birds. Getty Images Lobster Traps Like the cute chipmunk caught on the Cape, lobster traps in yards and at boat docks can end up as cages for wildlife that is out exploring.
Ellis told us that "rabbits especially get caught in lobster traps, both ornamental and stored for winter" adding owners need to "close up the entrance hole" when storing them to prevent anything other than lobsters from crawling inside. campbellphotostudio Fishing Line, Kite String and Balloon Ribbons One of the most common animal entanglements is fishing line, especially across the SouthCoast. Birds love to grab the fishing line, balloon ribbons and even kite string to use as nesting material. Ellis said she once even saw "a baby robin tethered to its nest by fishing line because its mother used it when building the nest."
She reminds everyone who breaks their line or kite string while out to take it with them and not just toss it aside on the ground. DigiStu Swimming Pools I'm sure there are many homeowners on the SouthCoast who have come home to find something swimming – or worse, floating – in their pool. Pools are super appealing to young frogs, baby salamanders and other wildlife, but once they are in, it can be difficult to get out.
"The best way to help animals out of the pool is to use a frog log or foam knee pad for gardening," Ellis said. Both can be attached to the side of the pool with one end in the water so animals that get in have a bridge to get themselves out. Much better than having to fish them out yourself. Sophie Bengtsson Blueberry Netting Actually, any netting for bushes in your yard can be dangerous to the wildlife running around. Sure, nets over the berry bushes are great for keeping the birds out, but as Ellis tells us, you usually end up with "a pile of netting at the bottom of the bush where snakes and frogs can get entangled."
She recommended "pulling the bottom taut so there isn't any excess or secure the bottom with zip ties so it's not bunching on the ground." I know I wouldn't want to come across a snake in my netting as I went to pick some berries. Nancy Hall/Townsquare Media Window Wells This one might be a yard danger you never really thought about, but for many SouthCoast homes, basement windows feature window wells, sunken space by the window usually framed in concrete.
Why are these dangerous? "Baby rabbits, turtles, salamanders and even young opossums can get stuck in these spaces," Ellis said. They hop in and then struggle to get back out. "Simply putting a stick in the well or a 2x4 piece of wood makes a ramp for something that gets caught in there," she said. Nancy Hall/Townsquare Media Buckets So many people have buckets floating in their yard for carrying things, doing yard work or whatever – but leaving your buckets open-end-up when not in use is a big no-no for keeping wildlife around your home safe.
Ellis reminds homeowners (and business owners) to turn buckets over to prevent critters from climbing in and getting stuck. can72 Christmas Decorations Christmas decorations are a tradition for many SouthCoast families, but they can cause some problems for wildlife. The bright lights can be a disturbance for critters living in your trees, so be mindful of them when choosing what to decorate or how long you leave the lights on at night.
Ellis also mentioned the danger of "small, edible pieces than animals may really try to eat." If fake berries are part of your outdoor decorations, try to display them where animals can't try to eat them for real. 4 Animals To be Hunted Year Round In Idaho According to this website . Animals You Can See Now At Zoo Boise Gallery Credit: Marco Marco, TSM Boise Gorongosa Exhibit One of my favorite parts of Zoo Boise is the new Gorongosa National Park Exhibit, a partnership between the zoo and the real Gorongosa National Park in Mozambique. The park in southeastern Africa was destroyed during a quarter-century of war in the region. Marco, TSM Boise Baboon This baboon is a part of the Gorongosa National Park Exhibit. Marco, TSM Boise Striped Hyena Even though the Striped Hyena looks and acts like a dog, it's genetically closer to a cat! Marco, TSM Boise African Wild Dog Part of the Gorongosa National Park Exhibit, the African Wild Dog, is on the endangered species list. Zoo Boise Crocodile Nile Crocodiles are found throughout Africa. The one at Zoo Boise is named Pandora! Marco, TSM Boise Patas Monkeys Patas Monkeys make different sounds to alert others when predators are near. They have a different sound for different types of danger. Zoo Boise Patas Monkey Zoo Boise Warthog Even though warthogs look intimidating, they are mostly plant-eaters. The most famous warthog is Pumbaa from the Lion King. Zoo Boise Southern Ground Hornbill This bird has a distinctive look and mostly eats small reptiles and frogs. Zoo Boise Nyala Male and female Nyala almost look like different animals! Zoo Boise Porcupine I always thought that porcupines could shoot their quills at attackers, but that isn't true. When disturbed, they raise their quills to make themselves appear larger and charge at their attacker running backward. Marco, TSM Boise Meerkat This cute little guy is a Slender-Tailed Meerkat. They live in burrows underground that can have 20 exits and entrances. Marco, TSM Boise Stellar's Sea Eagle Meet Vlad the Impaler! Vlad and fellow Stellar's Sea Eagle, Ursula, moved to Zoo Boise from the Denver Zoo in April. They are scarce birds of prey found in Japan and Russia. Zoo Boise Snow Leopard The Snow Leopard doesn't roar like other big cats, but they do hiss like a housecat! Marco, TSM Boise Tiger Diana is an Amur Tiger who came to Zoo Boise last year. She is one of 540 Amur Tigers left in the world. Marco, TSM Boise Sloth Bear The Sloth Bear was the inspiration for Baloo from the Jungle Book. Zoo Boise Lions Zoo Boise has African Lions. The most recent addition is a six-year-old male named Revan. He came to Boise a little over two years ago. Marco, TSM Boise Penguins Zoo Boise is home to a family of Magellanic Penguins. Jimmy and Rose had a baby boy chick in May 2020. You can see him pictured here. They welcomed baby girl, Daisy, in May 2021. Zoo Boise Two-Toed Sloth Sloth obsession is a real thing. Marco, TSM Boise Spider Monkeys One of the most prominent characters at Zoo Boise, Elvis, the Spider Monkey, is protective of the female zoo employees. Marco, TSM Boise Elvis the Spider Monkey Elvis has striking Blue eyes. Marco, TSM Boise Sarah the Spider Monkey Sarah, Zoo Boise's other Spider Monkey, resting in her tree.
